updates.title: OpenAI: new speak-up policy sends AI safety concerns to a board committee
updates.text: OpenAI replaced its Raising Concerns Policy on 30 October 2026. Staff can now take an AI safety concern straight to the Safety and Security Committee of the OpenAI Foundation's board, safety concerns raised through the anonymous Integrity Line are passed to that committee, and the policy says the committee has "full authority" to address them. "Safe internal channel" moves from B to A, so OpenAI's score goes from 43% to 46%. "Protected disclosures carved out" stays a C: the policy now covers former staff, but it still says it isn't a contract and doesn't say that no agreement overrides it.

updates.title: Anthropic: IPO filing makes its staff stock plan public
updates.text: Anthropic filed to go public on 26 October 2026, and the filing includes its staff stock plan. The plan says anyone fired "for Cause" loses all their unexercised stock options and all their restricted stock units, vested ones included. "Cause" includes "intentional material damage to the Company's business, property or reputation", and the company's decision on it is "final and binding". "Equity is never hostage" now cites the plan and stays a D: the plan has no stated exception for criticism or protected disclosures, but losing equity under it takes a for-Cause firing. "Protected disclosures carved out" also cites a severance agreement for executives from the same filing and stays a B. Scores are unchanged.

updates.title: Google DeepMind: former staff say raising the non-disparagement clause through formal routes changed nothing
updates.text: "Safe internal channel" now cites two accounts. Former research engineer Sofia Liguori told openDemocracy that an employee's attempts to raise the clause through internal channels led to no change. Andreas Kirsch has said he raised it in a formal protected disclosure in September 2026 and nothing changed, IBTimes UK reported. The grade stays a D. "Protected disclosures carved out" now notes that UK law voids a contract term so far as it tries to stop a protected disclosure, and stays "Not public". Scores are unchanged.

updates.title: xAI is now listed as xAI / SpaceXSI
updates.text: xAI now calls itself SpaceXSI (SpaceX Super Intelligence LLC); its terms of service, last updated on 27 October 2026, use that name. The scorecard now lists it as "xAI / SpaceXSI". Its page links and feed address changed with the name, and the old feed address redirects to the new one. No grade changed: "Whistleblowing policy is public" stays an F.

updates.title: Grades now run from A to F
updates.text: "Partly" was covering too much: 11 of the 17 ratings on staff contracts were "Partly", including all six of Anthropic's. Each clause is now split into three or four parts. "Meets" is an A and "Falls short" is an F. "Partly" is split into B (one part missing), C (in between) and D (only one part shown). "Not public" shows as "?" and still scores zero. A scores 1, B three quarters, C a half and D a quarter. No evidence changed. Google DeepMind's score moves from 7% to 4% because its "Safe internal channel" grade is a D. The evaluator tab is graded the same way, and Anthropic's score there moves from 42% to 33%.

updates.title: Google DeepMind: Google says new hires' non-disparagement terms no longer apply after they leave
updates.text: Google told the Washington Post on 3 November that it had recently removed "the post-termination aspect of non-disparagement clauses" from its terms for new hires, and that it doesn't enforce non-disparagement clauses after people leave. "No gag on criticism" now cites this and stays "Falls short": Google only described removing the part that applies after someone leaves, it didn't say existing contracts had changed, and the new wording isn't public. If Google publishes the wording, it will be rated on that wording. Scores are unchanged.

updates.title: New beta tab: what's public about labs' contracts with outside evaluators
updates.text: A second tab rates what's public about each lab's contracts with third-party evaluators, using the six terms in GovAI's proposal that these contracts be published: scope, access, publication rights, pay, conflict rules, and term and renewal. Anthropic scores 42% and OpenAI 33%, mostly "Partly" from their own announcements; Google DeepMind, xAI and Meta score 0% because nothing is public. No lab has published a full evaluation contract. These scores are separate and don't change the staff-contract scores.

updates.title: Google DeepMind: a former researcher posts the non-disparagement clause he signed
updates.text: Andreas Kirsch, a former Google DeepMind research scientist, posted on X a clause from the agreement he signed with Google in the UK in 2024. It says staff must not make "any statement" "criticising or disparaging Google", during or after employment, and he says it has no exemption for protected disclosures. "No gag on criticism" now cites it as its main source and stays "Falls short". A new entry for "Protected disclosures carved out" stays "Not public", because the rest of the agreement isn't public. Scores are unchanged.

updates.title: Lab Canary launched
updates.text: Five labs (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, xAI and Meta) rated on public evidence against seven clauses.

ratings.evidence: Its Responsible Scaling Policy commits that any non-disparagement clause won't stop staff or ex-staff publicly raising safety concerns. It doesn't rule out such clauses for other criticism.

A co-founder said vested equity was never tied to non-disparagement. Its RSP reporting policy prohibits retaliatory pay cuts and interference with earned benefits. Its stock plan, made public in its IPO filing on 26 Oct 2026, says anyone fired "for Cause" loses all their unexercised stock options and all their restricted stock units, vested ones included. "Cause" includes "intentional material damage to the Company's business, property or reputation", and the plan says the company decides this "in good faith" and its decision is "final and binding". The plan has no stated exception for criticism or protected disclosures. These sources don't establish protection against blocked equity sales for all criticism.

additionalSources.source: Anthropic RSP reporting and anti-retaliation policy
Anthropic 2021 Stock Plan and award agreements (IPO filing, Exhibit 10.4)

ratings.evidence: Its reporting policy says nothing in any Anthropic agreement stops staff reporting possible violations of law to government, without permission. That external-reporting clause does not expressly cover other concerns. A form of severance agreement for executives, in its IPO filing of 26 Oct 2026, says nothing in it stops the executive disclosing conduct they have reason to believe is unlawful. It covers executives only, and the confidentiality agreement it refers to isn't public.
ratings.source: Anthropic RSP reporting and anti-retaliation policy

additionalSources.source: Anthropic form of executive severance agreement (IPO filing, Exhibit 10.5)

ratings.evidence: Published an RSP whistleblowing policy in Dec 2025 and expanded reporting channels in Feb 2026. It covers RSP noncompliance; Anthropic says its broader reporting policy remains internal.
ratings.source: Anthropic RSP reporting and anti-retaliation policy

ratings.evidence: Anonymous reporting tool and a no-retaliation rule. Reports can go to an executive outside the safety officer's line, and the board gets quarterly updates. Not fully independent of leadership.
Its Responsible Scaling Policy permits disclosure of a non-disparagement clause's existence. The cited promise does not establish the same right for other types of agreement.

Vox reported in May 2024 that OpenAI's exit agreements barred ex-staff from criticising the company for life, at the risk of losing vested equity. OpenAI told Vox it had never cancelled anyone's vested equity. Days later, Bloomberg reported, OpenAI told former staff it would not cancel vested units, would release them from non-disparagement agreements unless the clause was mutual, and would remove the language from exit paperwork.
In May 2024, OpenAI said it would not cancel vested equity over criticism. That statement does not establish protection against withheld pay or blocked equity sales.

Its policy, last revised on 30 Oct 2026, says staff and former staff are always free to report concerns to an outside authority, without telling OpenAI first, and bans retaliation for giving information to any government body. It's “Partly” because the policy says it isn't a contract, and it doesn't say that no agreement overrides it or mention speaking to a lawyer. In 2024, whistleblowers alleged restrictive agreements hindered SEC reporting; OpenAI said its policy protected disclosures, TechCrunch reported.
Published a Raising Concerns Policy in Oct 2024, an expanded version in Jan 2026 and a revised version on 30 Oct 2026.

Anonymous Integrity Line, hosted by an outside provider, and a no-retaliation rule. Under the policy as revised on 30 Oct 2026, staff can take an AI safety concern straight to the Safety and Security Committee of the OpenAI Foundation's board, and safety concerns raised through the Integrity Line are passed to that committee, which has "full authority" to address them. Other reports go to OpenAI's Compliance team, which the policy says reports independently to the board's Audit Committee.

Contracts aren't public. The Register reported on 2 Oct 2026 that OpenAI had dismissed three staff, saying they mishandled sensitive company information. Some of it was allegedly shared with an outside AI evaluation group. OpenAI says the dismissals weren't about raising safety concerns. On 29 Oct 2026, 20 House Democrats wrote to OpenAI saying the three deny sharing confidential information, and asked what was shared and for a commitment not to fire whistleblowers.

additionalSources.source: Letter to OpenAI from Rep. Greg Casar and 19 other House Democrats

ratings.evidence: Vox reported in 2024 that even admitting the old exit agreement existed counted as a breach. Current terms aren't public.

Andreas Kirsch, a former Google DeepMind research scientist, posted on X a clause from the Confidentiality and Proprietary Information Agreement he signed with Google in the UK in 2024. It says that "at all times during employment and after the termination of employment" staff must not make "any statement" to anyone "criticising or disparaging Google". He says it has no exemption for protected disclosures. On 3 November 2026, Google told the Washington Post that it had recently removed "the post-termination aspect of non-disparagement clauses" from its terms for new hires, and that it doesn't enforce non-disparagement clauses after people leave. It described removing only the part that applies after someone leaves, didn't say existing contracts had changed, and hasn't published the new wording. Google employees also told the BBC that their contracts stop staff publicly criticising the company, and a research engineer who had just resigned said: "In principle I'm not allowed to criticise Google for the duration of my life." Google's statement to the BBC, as published, said staff have dedicated channels to raise concerns and that it prohibits retaliation. It didn't mention employment contracts. FLI's July 2026 index, partly using Google's private survey answers, gave Google 9 out of 10 for an explicit statement that NDAs and non-disparagement agreements can't stop safety-related whistleblowing.

additionalSources.source: Andreas Kirsch on X (no protected-disclosure exemption)

ratings.evidence: The non-disparagement clause Andreas Kirsch posted from his 2024 Google UK agreement has no exemption for protected disclosures, he says. The rest of the agreement isn't public, so it can't be checked whether another section carves them out. Under UK law, a contract term is void so far as it tries to stop a worker making a protected disclosure (Employment Rights Act 1996, section 43J), but the wording that's public doesn't tell staff that.

additionalSources.source: Employment Rights Act 1996, section 43J (in force since July 1999)

ratings.evidence: FLI's July 2026 review, using evidence up to 3 June, found no public whistleblowing policy. Google's Code of Conduct describes reporting channels and protection from retaliation.

Google says it has dedicated channels to raise concerns and anti-retaliation policies. Staff told the BBC people fear retaliation. Former research engineer Sofia Liguori told openDemocracy that an employee's attempts to raise the non-disparagement clause through internal channels led to no change. Andreas Kirsch has said he raised it in a formal protected disclosure in September 2026 and nothing changed, IBTimes UK reported.

xAI now calls itself SpaceXSI (SpaceX Super Intelligence LLC); its terms of service, last updated on 27 October 2026, use that name. In July 2026, The Midas Project reported no public whistleblowing policy. It reported that xAI's June framework revision removed earlier language on whistleblower protections and anonymous reporting. The December 2025 framework contained those commitments.

In March 2025, at Meta's request, an arbitrator issued an interim order temporarily barring a former Facebook director of global public policy from promoting her memoir, Careless People, while the arbitration continued. The arbitrator found Meta had a valid argument that she may have breached the non-disparagement agreement she signed when she left in 2017. Meta called the book a mix of out-of-date claims and false accusations. Meta's current terms aren't public.

FLI's July 2026 review, using evidence up to 3 June, found Meta's full whistleblowing policy was not public. Its October framework says a policy exists and further AI reporting procedures are being developed; it does not publish the full policy.
